title: Squares of a Sorted Array

concept.title: Two pointers from both ends
body: In a sorted array with negative numbers, the largest squares are at the **two ends**: a very negative number and a very positive number both have a big square. The smallest square is somewhere in the middle, near zero.
At each step the larger of the two end squares is the biggest square not yet placed, so you place it at the back of the result and move that pointer inward. No sorting is needed after squaring.

statement: You are given an array of `n` integers sorted in non-decreasing order. Print the squares of its elements, also sorted in non-decreasing order.
inputFormat: The second line has `n` integers in non-decreasing order.
hints: The biggest square is either at the left end or at the right end.
Use two pointers `l` and `r` and fill the result from the back.
Compare `abs(a[l])` with `abs(a[r])` and place the bigger square.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: The largest remaining square is always at one of the two ends. Placing it at the back and moving that pointer inward builds the sorted result in one pass.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

res = [0] * n
l, rr = 0, n - 1
for k in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    if abs(a[l]) > abs(a[rr]):
        res[k] = a[l] * a[l]
        l += 1
    else:
        res[k] = a[rr] * a[rr]
        rr -= 1
print(*res)
